title: Umar's night walks
hookLine: as caliph he walks at night and carries flour on his own back to a hungry family (reported)

cards: A fire, far out past the edge of Medina, in the dark. Two men walk toward it: Umar, now the caliph, the leader of the whole community, and Aslam, who served him. This story isn't in Bukhari or Muslim.
It's reported in later histories, told on Aslam's authority, and Muslims have passed it on for a long time. At the fire they find a woman and her children. The children are crying.
A pot is bubbling on the flames. Today: Umar's night walks.

teach.b: Umar asks what's in the pot. Water, she says. Only water.
She's stirring it so the children will think food is coming, until they cry themselves to sleep. Then, not knowing who she's talking to, she says: Allah will judge between us and Umar.
He's in charge of us, and he doesn't even know. Umar doesn't argue. He walks back to Medina, to the storehouse, and takes out flour and fat.
Put it on my back, he tells Aslam.
Aslam offers to carry it for him, and Umar answers with a question: will you carry my burden for me on the Day of Resurrection? So the ruler carries the flour out into the dark, on his own back.
In the report, he cooks for them himself, kneeling and blowing on the fire, until the food is ready and the children eat, and he stays until they're laughing and settle down.
The woman, still not knowing, tells him he's more fit for the job than the caliph. Whatever you make of the details, the story is built on something that is in Bukhari.

teach.h: EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.
teach.b: The Prophet said that each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock.

The ruler is a shepherd over his people. A man is a shepherd over his household, a woman in her husband's house. Umar heard the woman's line as a charge he would answer for, and the night walk was his answer.
Shepherds don't wait in the tent to be told a sheep is lost.

how: Muslims tell stories of Umar's night walks as examples of a ruler's responsibility, and often pair them with the hadith that each person is a shepherd responsible for those in their care.

games.q: you're Umar, the caliph. a stranger by a fire says her children are hungry and Umar doesn't even know. what do you do?
o: tell her who you are and promise help tomorrow.
send your servant back with some flour.
fetch the flour yourself and carry it on your back.
games.why: in the report, he carries it himself, cooks for them, and stays until the children are laughing.

practice: Think about your own small flock, the people who depend on you even a little: a child, a parent, a team, a neighbor, a friend going through it.
Walk its edges in your mind, the way Umar walked at night, and ask who might be stirring a pot of water right now, hoping nobody notices. If you pray, ask Allah to help you see who needs it.

wordCard.voice: Umar's night walks. A report in later histories: the caliph finds a hungry family at night and carries the flour to them on his own back. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a shepherd; from the hadith 'each of you is a shepherd'.

carryVoice: Your line: the ruler carried the flour. A caliph on his knees, blowing on a fire. Eight hundred two, done.

sources.ref: Report of Aslam, Umar's client (al-Tabari, Tarikh al-Rusul wa al-Muluk; Ibn al-Jawzi, Manaqib Umar)
